It was such a wrong move that even the band acknowledged that things went wrong, so they took some time off to regroup, issuing a hits collection Forever Delayed in 2002, with a B-sides and rarities comp Lipstick Traces following in 2003. The decks being suitably cleared, the band eased back in late 2004 with their seventh album Lifeblood, a record that takes the MOR/AOR inclinations of This Is My Truth Tell Me Yours to heart. Gliding by on smooth surfaces of synthesizers and lightly sequenced beats, Lifeblood is simpler and hookier than the lumbering Know Your Enemy, which is a relative blessing: it results in a record that's easier to enjoy, even if its smoothness doesn't gloss over memories of what the jagged, visceral band the Manics used to be. Even on the grandiose, arena-ready Everything Must Go, they sounded like a tense bundle of nerve and ambition, a clear byproduct of punk, but here they sound not far removed from the legions of po-faced, sincere but dull groups that stumbled through the colorless aftermath of Britpop at the tail-end of the '90s. Apart from a sense of craft that thoroughly identifies them as pros, what separates them now are what have always been their hallmarks: Nicky Wire 's perpetually adolescent literate literariness -- which, at this point, is either endearing or infuriating (though as lines like "so God is dead/like Nietzsche said" and titles like "The Love of Richard Nixon" pile up, it's hard not to tip toward the latter) -- and James Dean Bradfield 's keening, earnest vocals. When the music hit harder, Wire 's words made more sense and Bradfield 's singing tugged on the heartstrings, but with music as slick and seamless as this, they seem a touch anachronistic, the lone holdovers from when the band lived with abandon, giving their music an invigorating, reckless edge even when it was incoherent. But growing up was never going to be easy for the Manics -- they were either going to break up, embarrassingly ape their former glories (which they came perilously close to doing on Know Your Enemy ), or they were going to deliberately, somberly enter adulthood, as they do here. Since they craft solid records, Lifeblood is a pleasant listen, but once you peel away the keyboards, sensitively strummed guitars and tasteful harmonies and concentrate on Bradfield 's nakedly open voice and Wire 's terminally collegiate lyrics, it's hard to escape the unintentional pathos that winds up defining the album and, conceivably, the band's latter-day career. The Final Note SJC October 25, 2020 Dismissed by James Dean Bradfield as coinciding with a time in their artistic lives when the Manics were jaded, this album was nevertheless a partial return to form after the lack of direction of ‘Know Thy Enemy’. Yet, the synth-laden sound which permeates the album fails to deliver the necessary impact for Wire’s lyrics on songs eulogising Emily Pankhurst or addressing the horrors of 9/11. In the case of the latter, the track did start life on the festival circuit as a far edgier and rousing track, but got neutered in the studio. Even Wire miscalculated badly, tongue in cheek or not, when attempting to exonerate the character of Richard Nixon on the album’s quite bland leading single. Nevertheless, there are moments when this new musical avenue works really well such as on the notable tracks, ‘Always Never’ and ‘I Live to Fall Asleep’. Even more so when blended with their more traditional sound, such as an opener’1985’. This album requires a reassessment simply for containing the gems, ‘Glasnost’ and ‘Solitude Sometimes Is’. Certainly, the Manics had retreated to lick their wounds and issue the compilation ‘Forever Delayed’ two years earlier. it is a shame that the single which accompanied the latter, ‘There By the Grace of God’ did not grace this album as the lead single. After "Know your enemy" that contained the back-to-basics sound with rock leanings, "Lifeblood" is more polished and sonically less distinguishable effort. The first single, "The Love of Richard Nixon" is arguably their weakest hit song with a mediocre melody and simplified music structure. The only thing that stands out is the guitar solo. "Empty Souls" is a nod to their previous creativity - a powerful melody, the urge in the vocal and even lush piano textures. "A song for departure" confirms the polished pop orientation with piano being in the centre rather than guitar riffing. "To repel ghosts" sounds a bit cliche to me. Either have I heard that motive before or simply the song is not dinstinctive enough for the band of such calibre. "Emily" is, on the positive note, a graceful alternative pop ballad and belongs to the highlights. "Glasnost" is the most melodic piece on the album. The only further song that is worth mentioning is "Cardiff Afterlife" with great hooks and soothing mood. A good album but far from a masterpiece. Was this review helpful? It was such a wrong move that even the band acknowledged that things went wrong, so they took some time off to regroup, issuing a hits collection Forever Delayed in 2002, with a B-sides and rarities comp Lipstick Traces following in 2003. The decks being suitably cleared, the band eased back in late 2004 with their seventh album Lifeblood, a record that takes the MOR/AOR inclinations of This Is My Truth Tell Me Yours to heart. Gliding by on smooth surfaces of synthesizers and lightly sequenced beats, Lifeblood is simpler and hookier than the lumbering Know Your Enemy, which is a relative blessing: it results in a record that's easier to enjoy, even if its smoothness doesn't gloss over memories of what the jagged, visceral band the Manics used to be. Even on the grandiose, arena-ready Everything Must Go, they sounded like a tense bundle of nerve and ambition, a clear byproduct of punk, but here they sound not far removed from the legions of po-faced, sincere but dull groups that stumbled through the colorless aftermath of Britpop at the tail-end of the '90s. Apart from a sense of craft that thoroughly identifies them as pros, what separates them now are what have always been their hallmarks: Nicky Wire 's perpetually adolescent literate literariness -- which, at this point, is either endearing or infuriating (though as lines like "so God is dead/like Nietzsche said" and titles like "The Love of Richard Nixon" pile up, it's hard not to tip toward the latter) -- and James Dean Bradfield 's keening, earnest vocals. When the music hit harder, Wire 's words made more sense and Bradfield 's singing tugged on the heartstrings, but with music as slick and seamless as this, they seem a touch anachronistic, the lone holdovers from when the band lived with abandon, giving their music an invigorating, reckless edge even when it was incoherent. But growing up was never going to be easy for the Manics -- they were either going to break up, embarrassingly ape their former glories (which they came perilously close to doing on Know Your Enemy ), or they were going to deliberately, somberly enter adulthood, as they do here. Since they craft solid records, Lifeblood is a pleasant listen, but once you peel away the keyboards, sensitively strummed guitars and tasteful harmonies and concentrate on Bradfield 's nakedly open voice and Wire 's terminally collegiate lyrics, it's hard to escape the unintentional pathos that winds up defining the album and, conceivably, the band's latter-day career. The Final Note SJC October 25, 2020 Dismissed by James Dean Bradfield as coinciding with a time in their artistic lives when the Manics were jaded, this album was nevertheless a partial return to form after the lack of direction of ‘Know Thy Enemy’. Yet, the synth-laden sound which permeates the album fails to deliver the necessary impact for Wire’s lyrics on songs eulogising Emily Pankhurst or addressing the horrors of 9/11. In the case of the latter, the track did start life on the festival circuit as a far edgier and rousing track, but got neutered in the studio. Even Wire miscalculated badly, tongue in cheek or not, when attempting to exonerate the character of Richard Nixon on the album’s quite bland leading single. Nevertheless, there are moments when this new musical avenue works really well such as on the notable tracks, ‘Always Never’ and ‘I Live to Fall Asleep’. Even more so when blended with their more traditional sound, such as an opener’1985’. This album requires a reassessment simply for containing the gems, ‘Glasnost’ and ‘Solitude Sometimes Is’. Certainly, the Manics had retreated to lick their wounds and issue the compilation ‘Forever Delayed’ two years earlier. it is a shame that the single which accompanied the latter, ‘There By the Grace of God’ did not grace this album as the lead single. It was such a wrong move that even the band acknowledged that things went wrong, so they took some time off to regroup, issuing a hits collection Forever Delayed in 2002, with a B-sides and rarities comp Lipstick Traces following in 2003. The decks being suitably cleared, the band eased back in late 2004 with their seventh album Lifeblood, a record that takes the MOR/AOR inclinations of This Is My Truth Tell Me Yours to heart. Gliding by on smooth surfaces of synthesizers and lightly sequenced beats, Lifeblood is simpler and hookier than the lumbering Know Your Enemy, which is a relative blessing: it results in a record that's easier to enjoy, even if its smoothness doesn't gloss over memories of what the jagged, visceral band the Manics used to be. Even on the grandiose, arena-ready Everything Must Go, they sounded like a tense bundle of nerve and ambition, a clear byproduct of punk, but here they sound not far removed from the legions of po-faced, sincere but dull groups that stumbled through the colorless aftermath of Britpop at the tail-end of the '90s. Apart from a sense of craft that thoroughly identifies them as pros, what separates them now are what have always been their hallmarks: Nicky Wire 's perpetually adolescent literate literariness -- which, at this point, is either endearing or infuriating (though as lines like "so God is dead/like Nietzsche said" and titles like "The Love of Richard Nixon" pile up, it's hard not to tip toward the latter) -- and James Dean Bradfield 's keening, earnest vocals. When the music hit harder, Wire 's words made more sense and Bradfield 's singing tugged on the heartstrings, but with music as slick and seamless as this, they seem a touch anachronistic, the lone holdovers from when the band lived with abandon, giving their music an invigorating, reckless edge even when it was incoherent. But growing up was never going to be easy for the Manics -- they were either going to break up, embarrassingly ape their former glories (which they came perilously close to doing on Know Your Enemy ), or they were going to deliberately, somberly enter adulthood, as they do here. Since they craft solid records, Lifeblood is a pleasant listen, but once you peel away the keyboards, sensitively strummed guitars and tasteful harmonies and concentrate on Bradfield 's nakedly open voice and Wire 's terminally collegiate lyrics, it's hard to escape the unintentional pathos that winds up defining the album and, conceivably, the band's latter-day career. The Final Note SJC October 25, 2020 Dismissed by James Dean Bradfield as coinciding with a time in their artistic lives when the Manics were jaded, this album was nevertheless a partial return to form after the lack of direction of ‘Know Thy Enemy’. Yet, the synth-laden sound which permeates the album fails to deliver the necessary impact for Wire’s lyrics on songs eulogising Emily Pankhurst or addressing the horrors of 9/11. In the case of the latter, the track did start life on the festival circuit as a far edgier and rousing track, but got neutered in the studio. Even Wire miscalculated badly, tongue in cheek or not, when attempting to exonerate the character of Richard Nixon on the album’s quite bland leading single. Nevertheless, there are moments when this new musical avenue works really well such as on the notable tracks, ‘Always Never’ and ‘I Live to Fall Asleep’. Even more so when blended with their more traditional sound, such as an opener’1985’. This album requires a reassessment simply for containing the gems, ‘Glasnost’ and ‘Solitude Sometimes Is’. Certainly, the Manics had retreated to lick their wounds and issue the compilation ‘Forever Delayed’ two years earlier. it is a shame that the single which accompanied the latter, ‘There By the Grace of God’ did not grace this album as the lead single. It was such a wrong move that even the band acknowledged that things went wrong, so they took some time off to regroup, issuing a hits collection Forever Delayed in 2002, with a B-sides and rarities comp Lipstick Traces following in 2003. The decks being suitably cleared, the band eased back in late 2004 with their seventh album Lifeblood, a record that takes the MOR/AOR inclinations of This Is My Truth Tell Me Yours to heart. Gliding by on smooth surfaces of synthesizers and lightly sequenced beats, Lifeblood is simpler and hookier than the lumbering Know Your Enemy, which is a relative blessing: it results in a record that's easier to enjoy, even if its smoothness doesn't gloss over memories of what the jagged, visceral band the Manics used to be. Even on the grandiose, arena-ready Everything Must Go, they sounded like a tense bundle of nerve and ambition, a clear byproduct of punk, but here they sound not far removed from the legions of po-faced, sincere but dull groups that stumbled through the colorless aftermath of Britpop at the tail-end of the '90s. Apart from a sense of craft that thoroughly identifies them as pros, what separates them now are what have always been their hallmarks: Nicky Wire 's perpetually adolescent literate literariness -- which, at this point, is either endearing or infuriating (though as lines like "so God is dead/like Nietzsche said" and titles like "The Love of Richard Nixon" pile up, it's hard not to tip toward the latter) -- and James Dean Bradfield 's keening, earnest vocals. When the music hit harder, Wire 's words made more sense and Bradfield 's singing tugged on the heartstrings, but with music as slick and seamless as this, they seem a touch anachronistic, the lone holdovers from when the band lived with abandon, giving their music an invigorating, reckless edge even when it was incoherent. But growing up was never going to be easy for the Manics -- they were either going to break up, embarrassingly ape their former glories (which they came perilously close to doing on Know Your Enemy ), or they were going to deliberately, somberly enter adulthood, as they do here. Since they craft solid records, Lifeblood is a pleasant listen, but once you peel away the keyboards, sensitively strummed guitars and tasteful harmonies and concentrate on Bradfield 's nakedly open voice and Wire 's terminally collegiate lyrics, it's hard to escape the unintentional pathos that winds up defining the album and, conceivably, the band's latter-day career. The Final Note SJC October 25, 2020 Dismissed by James Dean Bradfield as coinciding with a time in their artistic lives when the Manics were jaded, this album was nevertheless a partial return to form after the lack of direction of ‘Know Thy Enemy’. Yet, the synth-laden sound which permeates the album fails to deliver the necessary impact for Wire’s lyrics on songs eulogising Emily Pankhurst or addressing the horrors of 9/11. In the case of the latter, the track did start life on the festival circuit as a far edgier and rousing track, but got neutered in the studio. Even Wire miscalculated badly, tongue in cheek or not, when attempting to exonerate the character of Richard Nixon on the album’s quite bland leading single. Nevertheless, there are moments when this new musical avenue works really well such as on the notable tracks, ‘Always Never’ and ‘I Live to Fall Asleep’. Even more so when blended with their more traditional sound, such as an opener’1985’. This album requires a reassessment simply for containing the gems, ‘Glasnost’ and ‘Solitude Sometimes Is’. Certainly, the Manics had retreated to lick their wounds and issue the compilation ‘Forever Delayed’ two years earlier. it is a shame that the single which accompanied the latter, ‘There By the Grace of God’ did not grace this album as the lead single. After "Know your enemy" that contained the back-to-basics sound with rock leanings, "Lifeblood" is more polished and sonically less distinguishable effort. The first single, "The Love of Richard Nixon" is arguably their weakest hit song with a mediocre melody and simplified music structure. The only thing that stands out is the guitar solo. "Empty Souls" is a nod to their previous creativity - a powerful melody, the urge in the vocal and even lush piano textures. "A song for departure" confirms the polished pop orientation with piano being in the centre rather than guitar riffing. "To repel ghosts" sounds a bit cliche to me. Either have I heard that motive before or simply the song is not dinstinctive enough for the band of such calibre. "Emily" is, on the positive note, a graceful alternative pop ballad and belongs to the highlights. "Glasnost" is the most melodic piece on the album. The only further song that is worth mentioning is "Cardiff Afterlife" with great hooks and soothing mood. A good album but far from a masterpiece. Was this review helpful? The Final Note SJC November 23, 2020 The Manics will be rightfully regarded by music historians as one of the greatest bands of all time, and one in perpetual motion between maintaining loyalty to their punk roots and producing grandiose concert arena rock anthems. One hopes that their wide legions of devout fans will look back on albums such as this with as much, if not more, appreciation as ‘The Holy Bible’. Nicky Wire proudly promoted this work as sounding like ‘heavy metal Tamla Motown’, while Bradfield openly confessed that they were seeking commercial and chart success. straight out of the blocks, comes one of their greatest compositions, ‘(It’s Not War) Just the End of Love’ with soaring strings matched by Bradfield’s guitar. Other highlights include the title track which encapsulates the band’s attempts to reconcile the idealism and principles of their youth with their more mellow and mature selves, and their wish to make political statement through music to the pure simple joy of producing music. ‘Hamlet on Avenue’, “Golden Platitudes’ and ‘I Think I Found It’ continue the series of slick melodies which pepper the album. One is even prepared to accept the OTT wonder that is ‘Some Kind of Nothingness’ where Bradfield duets with Ian McCullough. Yet, together with the aforementioned opener, this reviewer would applaud the grittier blending of harmony with post-punk in ‘Auto-Intoxication’. Was this review helpful? Everything Must Go was cathartic, the bandmembers exorcizing their grief after the disappearance of Richey Edwards, but Postcards from a Young Man is as celebratory as the Manics get, a record that recklessly flirts with joyousness. Once again, the band abandons coiled, tense art-punk for anthemic stadium-fillers, creating arrangements so overloaded they threaten to collapse in a tower of sitars, strings, mandolins, fuzz guitars, and cameos from Ian McCulloch and Duff McKagan . The presence of an Echo & the Bunnyman and a Guns N' Roses is typical of the Manics’ almost ludicrous overreach: they blend moody Englishness with American hooks, which has been their plan since the outset, but they’ve rarely been as successful as they are on Postcards from a Young Man simply because they let their penchant for exaggeration run wild. With the notable exception of Nicky Wire ’s lyrics -- whose small scale almost seems like a relief after the airing of Edwards ’ unused words on Journal -- everything here is bigger than usual, the rhythms packing an unusual swing, the productions scraping the sky, and the hooks spilling out of James Dean Bradfield ’s mouth and guitar alike. All this bustle winds up being the rarest of things for the Manics: it is fun. Granted, it is serious-minded fun with ambition, but with Manic Street Preachers you take fun whenever you can get it, and they’ve never sounded as ebullient as they do here. The Final Note SJC November 23, 2020 The Manics will be rightfully regarded by music historians as one of the greatest bands of all time, and one in perpetual motion between maintaining loyalty to their punk roots and producing grandiose concert arena rock anthems. One hopes that their wide legions of devout fans will look back on albums such as this with as much, if not more, appreciation as ‘The Holy Bible’. Nicky Wire proudly promoted this work as sounding like ‘heavy metal Tamla Motown’, while Bradfield openly confessed that they were seeking commercial and chart success. straight out of the blocks, comes one of their greatest compositions, ‘(It’s Not War) Just the End of Love’ with soaring strings matched by Bradfield’s guitar. Other highlights include the title track which encapsulates the band’s attempts to reconcile the idealism and principles of their youth with their more mellow and mature selves, and their wish to make political statement through music to the pure simple joy of producing music. ‘Hamlet on Avenue’, “Golden Platitudes’ and ‘I Think I Found It’ continue the series of slick melodies which pepper the album. One is even prepared to accept the OTT wonder that is ‘Some Kind of Nothingness’ where Bradfield duets with Ian McCullough. Yet, together with the aforementioned opener, this reviewer would applaud the grittier blending of harmony with post-punk in ‘Auto-Intoxication’. Was this review helpful? That record wound up closing an era where the Manics looked back toward their own history as a way of moving forward, but Futurology definitively opens a new chapter for the Welsh trio, one where they're pushing into uncharted territory. Never mind that, by most standards this charge toward the future is also predicated on the past, with the group finding fuel within the robotic rhythms of Krautrock and the arty fallout of punk; within the context of the Manics, this is a bracing, necessary shift in direction. All the death disco, free-range electronics, Low homages, and Teutonic grooves, suit the situational politics of the Manics, perhaps even better than the AOR-inspired anthems that have been their stock in trade, but the words -- crafted, as ever, by Nicky Wire, who remains obsessed with self-recriminations, injustice and rallying cries -- aren't the focus here. Unique among Manics albums, Futurology is primarily about the music, with the surging synthesizers and jagged arrangements providing not an emotional blood-letting or call to arms, but rather an internal journey. At times, this is broad, expansive rock & roll, possessed by insistent four-four rhythms unheard in the group's discography, but when the Manics do dip into disco -- as they do several times, most prominently on "Sex, Power, Love and Money" and "Dreaming a City" -- they're underscoring how they're making music for the head and the heart, not the feet or loins. That's also why Green Gartside is such a welcome presence on "Between the Clock and the Bed": his Scritti Politti managed the divide between radical art and commercial pop, providing a touchstone for the Manics even if they rarely specifically mimic his sound. They're more infatuated with Neu! and Kraftwerk or Public Image Ltd, but these jagged, difficult sounds are filtered through the trio's now instinctual arena-filling gestures and that tension is what gives Futurology a resonant richness. The Manics aren't ditching what they are, they're building upon it and finding an invigorating path into middle age. Murray Winship April 6, 2025 Manic Street Preachers are politically charged Welsh rockers with a complex history and a remarkable evolution into intelligent, accessible alternative pop. Their 2025 release, "Critical Thinking," delivers an exceptional sound, showcasing cohesion and harmony like never before—perhaps even reminiscent of U2. Their music is truly enjoyable and thought-provoking, perfect for inspiring some "Critical Thinking" of your own. Pax, Murf Was this review helpful? Yes ( 3 ) No ( 1 ) Report Inappropriate Lucky Medan April 7, 2025 Manics is one of my favorite bands of all time but, using my "critical thinking", I have mixed feelings about this record: I like the songs, although it's not the best collection they've released. But I don't like the sound, it has a flat, compressed, saturated and noisy production (dinamic compression, the famous loudness war), with excessive reverb, drums muffled off and a lot of instrumental filler that drowns out the freshness of the songs. To enhance these songs, you need a visceral guitar playing and fewer layers of filler sound. Regarding the recording studios for Critical Thinking, like the last albums, it was done in the Manic Street Preachers' own studios (Door To The River) and Rockfield Studios(Wales). They would certainly improve in the future if they moved away from their comfort zone and producer Dave Eringa, and went to record away from home with another producer. The last album they did this was "Futurology", and you can tell the difference for the better on that album. But "The Ultra Vivid Lament" and "Critical Thinking" have been number 1 or 2 in the U.K., so unfortunately we will continue to have Dave Eringa as the Manics' producer in the future. I like the album, like everything they have released in the past, but I don't love it. I prefer the Deluxe Edition, which includes all the songs in demo form, which I generally like better than the final versions. Also, the Deluxe Edition has handwritten lyrics. P.S.: A year after purchasing and listening to Critical Thinking repeatedly, I must say it's a good album, despite its sonic flaws. But please, take a few more risks on the next album. Choose a different producer and studio. I can't wait. Was this review helpful? Murray Winship April 6, 2025 Manic Street Preachers are politically charged Welsh rockers with a complex history and a remarkable evolution into intelligent, accessible alternative pop. Their 2025 release, "Critical Thinking," delivers an exceptional sound, showcasing cohesion and harmony like never before—perhaps even reminiscent of U2. Their music is truly enjoyable and thought-provoking, perfect for inspiring some "Critical Thinking" of your own. Pax, Murf Was this review helpful? Yes ( 3 ) No ( 1 ) Report Inappropriate Lucky Medan April 7, 2025 Manics is one of my favorite bands of all time but, using my "critical thinking", I have mixed feelings about this record: I like the songs, although it's not the best collection they've released. But I don't like the sound, it has a flat, compressed, saturated and noisy production (dinamic compression, the famous loudness war), with excessive reverb, drums muffled off and a lot of instrumental filler that drowns out the freshness of the songs. To enhance these songs, you need a visceral guitar playing and fewer layers of filler sound. Regarding the recording studios for Critical Thinking, like the last albums, it was done in the Manic Street Preachers' own studios (Door To The River) and Rockfield Studios(Wales). They would certainly improve in the future if they moved away from their comfort zone and producer Dave Eringa, and went to record away from home with another producer. The last album they did this was "Futurology", and you can tell the difference for the better on that album. But "The Ultra Vivid Lament" and "Critical Thinking" have been number 1 or 2 in the U.K., so unfortunately we will continue to have Dave Eringa as the Manics' producer in the future. I like the album, like everything they have released in the past, but I don't love it. I prefer the Deluxe Edition, which includes all the songs in demo form, which I generally like better than the final versions. Also, the Deluxe Edition has handwritten lyrics. P.S.: A year after purchasing and listening to Critical Thinking repeatedly, I must say it's a good album, despite its sonic flaws. But please, take a few more risks on the next album. Choose a different producer and studio. I can't wait. Was this review helpful? Murray Winship April 6, 2025 Manic Street Preachers are politically charged Welsh rockers with a complex history and a remarkable evolution into intelligent, accessible alternative pop. Their 2025 release, "Critical Thinking," delivers an exceptional sound, showcasing cohesion and harmony like never before—perhaps even reminiscent of U2. Their music is truly enjoyable and thought-provoking, perfect for inspiring some "Critical Thinking" of your own. Pax, Murf Was this review helpful? Yes ( 3 ) No ( 1 ) Report Inappropriate Lucky Medan April 7, 2025 Manics is one of my favorite bands of all time but, using my "critical thinking", I have mixed feelings about this record: I like the songs, although it's not the best collection they've released. But I don't like the sound, it has a flat, compressed, saturated and noisy production (dinamic compression, the famous loudness war), with excessive reverb, drums muffled off and a lot of instrumental filler that drowns out the freshness of the songs. To enhance these songs, you need a visceral guitar playing and fewer layers of filler sound. Regarding the recording studios for Critical Thinking, like the last albums, it was done in the Manic Street Preachers' own studios (Door To The River) and Rockfield Studios(Wales). They would certainly improve in the future if they moved away from their comfort zone and producer Dave Eringa, and went to record away from home with another producer. The last album they did this was "Futurology", and you can tell the difference for the better on that album. But "The Ultra Vivid Lament" and "Critical Thinking" have been number 1 or 2 in the U.K., so unfortunately we will continue to have Dave Eringa as the Manics' producer in the future. I like the album, like everything they have released in the past, but I don't love it. I prefer the Deluxe Edition, which includes all the songs in demo form, which I generally like better than the final versions. Also, the Deluxe Edition has handwritten lyrics. P.S.: A year after purchasing and listening to Critical Thinking repeatedly, I must say it's a good album, despite its sonic flaws. But please, take a few more risks on the next album. Choose a different producer and studio. I can't wait. Was this review helpful? (1998) Nuisance Review by AllMusic Nuisance Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine Perhaps Menswear was always destined to be a footnote in pop history, a product of the heady good times of London in 1994 and 1995. Reportedly signed after only three shows, the band was never given the chance to fully develop before they recorded their debut album, Nuisance. At the time of their first single, they appropriated the sound of Blur and the style of Pulp ; by the time Nuisance was released, they also incorporated the sound of Elastica and Oasis, making the band a virtual Cliff Notes of Brit-pop. Naturally, Menswear doesn't quite have the skills or panache of any of their idols, but that doesn't mean they are lacking in charm. Like Oasis and Blur, Menswear appropriates sections of pop history, claiming them as their own. However, they aren't half the songwriters that Noel Gallagher and Damon Albarn are, which means many of their ideas are never developed. Nevertheless, when they assimilate them fully -- like the intoxicating rush of "Around You Again" or the sweeping ballad "Being Brave," which lifts the intro to Pink Floyd 's "Comfortably Numb" -- the band is an undeniable guilty pleasure. When pressed, the 'swear can come up with irresistably infectious pop gems, from the frazzled Monkees pop of "Sleeping In" to the flat-out great single "Daydreamer," which sounds more like Wire than Elastica, only funnier, even if it may be unintentional. Even funnier are Johnny Dean 's lyrics, from the groupie saga of "125 West 3rd Street" to "Stardust," a silly attack on Primal Scream 's Bobby Gillespie . In all, Nuisance is the perfect product from a band that is better known for being seen than being heard. At the time of their 1995 debut, Nuisance, they were historically criticized for being a rehash of other Britpop bands at the time, having mostly rhyme-based, meaningless lyrics about bizarre everyday conversations (“Tess, he said, I don't understand / How they grow tomatoes in a can / Tess, he said, now wait a while / My teeth don't glitter when I smile”), and barely got any retrospective review later. Tracks consist of swinging rips from Lynyrd Skynyrd’s “Sweet Home Alabama” and The Charlatans (“125 West 3rd Street”, “Hollywood Girl”), funky grooves with extended seventh-chording (“I'll Manage Somehow”), droning A-major post-psychedelia (“Sleeping In”), psychotic, half-wailed dissonance (“Little Miss Pinpoint Eyes”, the T. Rex-derived “Daydreamer”, the showy “Stardust”) and rare, longer, calmer balladry reminiscent of Love at their most orchestral (“Being Brave”, “Piece of Me”). The merging of Pop Punk Ramones-like power-chording with more dramatic strings on “The One” doesn’t really work, and there’s not a lot of highlights beyond several steps in revival, triumphant arrangements and hooks. Both overvalued and undervalued. Not a great album, nor a bad one: just a generic one, with hints of weirdness and arrogance not to suggest total oblivion. Highlights: “I'll Manage Somehow”, “Daydreamer”. Was this review helpful? (1998) ¡Hay Tiempo! Review by AllMusic ¡Hay Tiempo! Review by Jason Damas To most, Menswear's 1996 one-off single We Love You was the band's swan song. However, despite being dropped by their record company in every country but Japan, Menswear still managed to release their second album, Hay Tiempo, in that country. This record, however, was hardly what anyone would expect from them. More or less abandoning their stylized, loud pop formula, Hay Tiempo is much more rooted in trad rock, with no less than three five-plus minute opuses in the middle of a ten-song cycle. The disc is a textbook sophomore slump; Menswear was essentially a singles band, yet there are not many standout tracks here. The more aggressive songs, for the most part, sound bland and uninspired, with the sole exception of "Waiting for the Sun," which evokes some of the joys found in their debut. The songs that do stand out are mostly the ballads, like the orchestral opener "Every Sound's a Melody" and the excellent "Coming Home," essentially a rewrite of the previous album's "Being Brave." "Coming Home" is not only the best track on the album, but was unfortunately also the band's subtle wave goodbye; shortly after the release of Hay Tiempo they permanently disbanded. This disc does have a few virtues, however, the most notable being that it does, surprisingly, hold up better upon repeat listens. This alone makes it a worthwhile buy for hardcore fans of the band, even though the price and relative obscurity of each copy is a sizable obstacle. Hay Tiempo may not have been the best way for Menswear to say goodbye, but it is a set of ten songs that may please die-hard fans. ¡Hay Tiempo! Review by AllMusic (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine If Definitely Maybe was an unintentional concept album about wanting to be a rock & roll star, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? is what happens after the dreams come true. Oasis turns in a relatively introspective second record, filled with big, gorgeous ballads instead of ripping rockers. Unlike Definitely Maybe, the production on Morning Glory is varied enough to handle the range in emotions; instead of drowning everything with amplifiers turned up to 12, there are strings, keyboards, and harmonicas. This expanded production helps give Noel Gallagher 's sweeping melodies an emotional resonance that he occasionally can't convey lyrically. However, that is far from a fatal flaw; Gallagher 's lyrics work best in fragments, where the images catch in your mind and grow, thanks to the music. Gallagher may be guilty of some borrowing, or even plagiarism, but he uses the familiar riffs as building blocks. This is where his genius lies: He's a thief and doesn't have many original thoughts, but as a pop/rock melodicist he's pretty much without peer. Likewise, as musicians, Oasis are hardly innovators, yet they have a majestic grandeur in their sound that makes ballads like "Wonderwall" or rockers like "Some Might Say" positively transcendent. Alan White does add authority to the rhythm section, but the most noticeable change is in Liam Gallagher . His voice sneered throughout Definitely Maybe, but on Morning Glory his singing has become more textured and skillful. He gives the lyric in the raging title track a hint of regret, is sympathetic on "Wonderwall," defiant on "Some Might Say," and humorous on "She's Electric," a bawdy rewrite of "Digsy's Diner." It might not have the immediate impact of Definitely Maybe, but Morning Glory is just as exciting and compulsively listenable. (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Peter Humphreys January 14, 2017 Oasis fans tend to fall into two camps – those that believe their debut album “Definitely Maybe” was their best work, and those that think their monster follow up, “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory” took the cake. (Maybe there are some people who came late on the scene who put in a good word for “Dig Out Your Soul”, or “Don’t Believe the Truth”, but I haven’t met them.) I am squarely in the “Morning Glory” camp. Yes, “Definitely Maybe” was a wonderfully sharp rocker, but “Morning Glory” defined a genre. Whenever anyone talks about Britpop, you can’t do it without talking about this album – it is the benchmark. There would be no Britpop if Oasis had stopped after album number one (although Britrock maybe?). And as influential as Blur, Suede and Pulp were to the genre and to popular music generally, even though they all had albums predating Oasis, they weren’t really part of the movement until “Morning Glory” came along. “Morning Glory” gave Britpop momentum. “Morning Glory” has a particular sound, amazingly fresh when you consider how much Noel Gallagher borrowed from others – the wonderful “Don’t Look Back In Anger” leads to a towering chorus that John Lennon’s “Imagine” never got close to achieving, despite the two songs starting with the same piano riff, and Gary Glitter gets co-writing credits on opening track “Hello”, presumably so Noel Gallagher could avoid yet another songwriter taking him to court for pinching one of their songs. Each song is different, and is strong enough to be a hit (if you ignore the two 60-second untitled instrumental tracks), but each one feels like it belongs on the album, and that it is a perfect marriage of music and lyrics. When it comes to it, an album is an entity, designed to be heard in its entirety – yet an album of popular music needs to be able to be broken down into individual songs that are strong enough to stand alone. “Morning Glory” is one of those rare beasts that succeeds on both levels, and one that will always have defined a genre of its time. Was this review helpful? Yes ( 1 ) No ( 1 ) Report Inappropriate James Taylor September 27, 2021 This record defined 1995: I remember hearing it at home, at school, at parties... In the end it came to define mid-nineties culture in the UK in a way that today seems quaint. Imagine if 2020’s major headlines concerned the CD sales, supposed rivalries and off-stage antics of a rock band. This period will always be referred to as peak ‘Britpop.’ I always hated that label, mainly because it lumped bands together that otherwise had no connection besides having formed in the UK, as if nationality were a musical genre and all British groups — whether from London, Liverpool, or even Manchester — sought the same sound. It also meant that many mediocre imitation bands got to bask in the glow of fame earned by the more talented ones, resulting in clogged airwaves and an increasingly tiresome scene (I felt British music became notably looser and more varied once the media frenzy had faded by the end of the decade). “Morning Glory” is not my favourite Oasis album (that distinction still belongs to “Be Here Now,” much to the disbelief of most). But a quarter-century later it still sounds great and I still know every word, though I cannot disassociate it from endless days of cloud and drizzle. Noel Gallagher’s lyrics were always self-aware but vague, as if he was recalling a dream from a few nights before but also looking ahead a couple of decades, imagining a nostalgia for something that had yet to happen. Like a professional athlete, he seemed conscious of the fact that success would be fleeting, that the giant wave his band rode by nature could not last, and that this was his personal moment in pop history. I think that slight urgency gave Oasis an edge over their contemporaries, whose clever posturing and arch humour perhaps had less direct appeal. They also simply wrote better songs (though they still never really “cracked” America). Anyway, it’s getting late, tomorrow is Saturday, and I need a little time to wake up, wake up... The album kicks off with Hello, which is a perfect opener. The recording sounds great, length is good, however I don't think the record should have opened with the bit from Wonderwall, which is actually a recording of Noel playing it on a wall outside of Rockfield Studios, where the majority of the album was recorded. (There's also a funny story of Bonehead driving a remote control car to disturb him. Not sure what Noel was thinking) Next is "Roll With It." This is a weak point on the album. The melody is overwhelmingly cheesy, but Alan White's drum work is good. "Wonderwall" is obviously Oasis' most popular song, and it really does not have any flaws. I love how the bass isolated is so crunchy and distorted, but sounds great in the mix. Liam's vocals are right in your face and are sung with such attitude. "Don't Look Back in Anger" is next, which in my opinion is Oasis' best song. Everything about this song is perfect. Noel's vocal sounds aggressive yet graceful, making for a rocking ballad. After this is "Hey Now!", which is undeniably a weak point. It is too long, however the lyrics are enjoyable and easy to understand, even with Liam's Lydon-esque snarl and Mancunian accent. Next is "Some Might Say." This song is great aside from Tony McCarroll's drumming. Liam sounds insane, probably one of the biggest highlights of his vocal career. "Cast No Shadow" has a very prominent bassline which I appreciate, but the melody seems to be repeated too many times. Alan's decision to use hot rods as he did on Wonderwall is a very nice touch. "She's Electric" sounds like a straight Beatles outtake, however Liam delivers once again. Next is "Morning Glory," which is a rocking song, but suffers from the most brickwalling in audio history. Towards the end of the song everything sounds like it is being crushed and distorted like crazy. You can also barely hear the drums, with no punch. It feels like Owen Morris, the producer, took ambience and reverb over definition, utilizing lots of room mics or mixing them much higher than close ones. Again, Liam sounds monstrous and absolutely carries the track. The album ends with "Champagne Supernova" which is a perfect ending. Paul Weller carries this track, but the lyrics prevent it from being a classic for me. The swirl at the end is perfect though and HERE there is appropriate punch on Alan's drums. That's what happens when Noel doesn't leave 20 tracks of guitar and actually gives space. Overall, the audio quality on this album is INSANELY compressed. There is no dynamic range in Liam's vocals, but that fits his in-your-face style of singing. This doesn't take away from the fact that this album is filled with great songs, but prevents it from deserving a 5 star review. Was this review helpful? Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine If Definitely Maybe was an unintentional concept album about wanting to be a rock & roll star, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? is what happens after the dreams come true. Oasis turns in a relatively introspective second record, filled with big, gorgeous ballads instead of ripping rockers. Unlike Definitely Maybe, the production on Morning Glory is varied enough to handle the range in emotions; instead of drowning everything with amplifiers turned up to 12, there are strings, keyboards, and harmonicas. This expanded production helps give Noel Gallagher 's sweeping melodies an emotional resonance that he occasionally can't convey lyrically. However, that is far from a fatal flaw; Gallagher 's lyrics work best in fragments, where the images catch in your mind and grow, thanks to the music. Gallagher may be guilty of some borrowing, or even plagiarism, but he uses the familiar riffs as building blocks. This is where his genius lies: He's a thief and doesn't have many original thoughts, but as a pop/rock melodicist he's pretty much without peer. Likewise, as musicians, Oasis are hardly innovators, yet they have a majestic grandeur in their sound that makes ballads like "Wonderwall" or rockers like "Some Might Say" positively transcendent. Alan White does add authority to the rhythm section, but the most noticeable change is in Liam Gallagher . His voice sneered throughout Definitely Maybe, but on Morning Glory his singing has become more textured and skillful. He gives the lyric in the raging title track a hint of regret, is sympathetic on "Wonderwall," defiant on "Some Might Say," and humorous on "She's Electric," a bawdy rewrite of "Digsy's Diner." It might not have the immediate impact of Definitely Maybe, but Morning Glory is just as exciting and compulsively listenable. (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Peter Humphreys January 14, 2017 Oasis fans tend to fall into two camps – those that believe their debut album “Definitely Maybe” was their best work, and those that think their monster follow up, “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory” took the cake. (Maybe there are some people who came late on the scene who put in a good word for “Dig Out Your Soul”, or “Don’t Believe the Truth”, but I haven’t met them.) I am squarely in the “Morning Glory” camp. Yes, “Definitely Maybe” was a wonderfully sharp rocker, but “Morning Glory” defined a genre. Whenever anyone talks about Britpop, you can’t do it without talking about this album – it is the benchmark. There would be no Britpop if Oasis had stopped after album number one (although Britrock maybe?). And as influential as Blur, Suede and Pulp were to the genre and to popular music generally, even though they all had albums predating Oasis, they weren’t really part of the movement until “Morning Glory” came along. “Morning Glory” gave Britpop momentum. “Morning Glory” has a particular sound, amazingly fresh when you consider how much Noel Gallagher borrowed from others – the wonderful “Don’t Look Back In Anger” leads to a towering chorus that John Lennon’s “Imagine” never got close to achieving, despite the two songs starting with the same piano riff, and Gary Glitter gets co-writing credits on opening track “Hello”, presumably so Noel Gallagher could avoid yet another songwriter taking him to court for pinching one of their songs. Each song is different, and is strong enough to be a hit (if you ignore the two 60-second untitled instrumental tracks), but each one feels like it belongs on the album, and that it is a perfect marriage of music and lyrics. When it comes to it, an album is an entity, designed to be heard in its entirety – yet an album of popular music needs to be able to be broken down into individual songs that are strong enough to stand alone. “Morning Glory” is one of those rare beasts that succeeds on both levels, and one that will always have defined a genre of its time. Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine If Definitely Maybe was an unintentional concept album about wanting to be a rock & roll star, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? is what happens after the dreams come true. Oasis turns in a relatively introspective second record, filled with big, gorgeous ballads instead of ripping rockers. Unlike Definitely Maybe, the production on Morning Glory is varied enough to handle the range in emotions; instead of drowning everything with amplifiers turned up to 12, there are strings, keyboards, and harmonicas. This expanded production helps give Noel Gallagher 's sweeping melodies an emotional resonance that he occasionally can't convey lyrically. However, that is far from a fatal flaw; Gallagher 's lyrics work best in fragments, where the images catch in your mind and grow, thanks to the music. Gallagher may be guilty of some borrowing, or even plagiarism, but he uses the familiar riffs as building blocks. This is where his genius lies: He's a thief and doesn't have many original thoughts, but as a pop/rock melodicist he's pretty much without peer. Likewise, as musicians, Oasis are hardly innovators, yet they have a majestic grandeur in their sound that makes ballads like "Wonderwall" or rockers like "Some Might Say" positively transcendent. Alan White does add authority to the rhythm section, but the most noticeable change is in Liam Gallagher . His voice sneered throughout Definitely Maybe, but on Morning Glory his singing has become more textured and skillful. He gives the lyric in the raging title track a hint of regret, is sympathetic on "Wonderwall," defiant on "Some Might Say," and humorous on "She's Electric," a bawdy rewrite of "Digsy's Diner." It might not have the immediate impact of Definitely Maybe, but Morning Glory is just as exciting and compulsively listenable. (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Peter Humphreys January 14, 2017 Oasis fans tend to fall into two camps – those that believe their debut album “Definitely Maybe” was their best work, and those that think their monster follow up, “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory” took the cake. (Maybe there are some people who came late on the scene who put in a good word for “Dig Out Your Soul”, or “Don’t Believe the Truth”, but I haven’t met them.) I am squarely in the “Morning Glory” camp. Yes, “Definitely Maybe” was a wonderfully sharp rocker, but “Morning Glory” defined a genre. Whenever anyone talks about Britpop, you can’t do it without talking about this album – it is the benchmark. There would be no Britpop if Oasis had stopped after album number one (although Britrock maybe?). And as influential as Blur, Suede and Pulp were to the genre and to popular music generally, even though they all had albums predating Oasis, they weren’t really part of the movement until “Morning Glory” came along. “Morning Glory” gave Britpop momentum. “Morning Glory” has a particular sound, amazingly fresh when you consider how much Noel Gallagher borrowed from others – the wonderful “Don’t Look Back In Anger” leads to a towering chorus that John Lennon’s “Imagine” never got close to achieving, despite the two songs starting with the same piano riff, and Gary Glitter gets co-writing credits on opening track “Hello”, presumably so Noel Gallagher could avoid yet another songwriter taking him to court for pinching one of their songs. Each song is different, and is strong enough to be a hit (if you ignore the two 60-second untitled instrumental tracks), but each one feels like it belongs on the album, and that it is a perfect marriage of music and lyrics. When it comes to it, an album is an entity, designed to be heard in its entirety – yet an album of popular music needs to be able to be broken down into individual songs that are strong enough to stand alone. “Morning Glory” is one of those rare beasts that succeeds on both levels, and one that will always have defined a genre of its time. Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine If Definitely Maybe was an unintentional concept album about wanting to be a rock & roll star, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? is what happens after the dreams come true. Oasis turns in a relatively introspective second record, filled with big, gorgeous ballads instead of ripping rockers. Unlike Definitely Maybe, the production on Morning Glory is varied enough to handle the range in emotions; instead of drowning everything with amplifiers turned up to 12, there are strings, keyboards, and harmonicas. This expanded production helps give Noel Gallagher 's sweeping melodies an emotional resonance that he occasionally can't convey lyrically. However, that is far from a fatal flaw; Gallagher 's lyrics work best in fragments, where the images catch in your mind and grow, thanks to the music. Gallagher may be guilty of some borrowing, or even plagiarism, but he uses the familiar riffs as building blocks. This is where his genius lies: He's a thief and doesn't have many original thoughts, but as a pop/rock melodicist he's pretty much without peer. Likewise, as musicians, Oasis are hardly innovators, yet they have a majestic grandeur in their sound that makes ballads like "Wonderwall" or rockers like "Some Might Say" positively transcendent. Alan White does add authority to the rhythm section, but the most noticeable change is in Liam Gallagher . His voice sneered throughout Definitely Maybe, but on Morning Glory his singing has become more textured and skillful. He gives the lyric in the raging title track a hint of regret, is sympathetic on "Wonderwall," defiant on "Some Might Say," and humorous on "She's Electric," a bawdy rewrite of "Digsy's Diner." It might not have the immediate impact of Definitely Maybe, but Morning Glory is just as exciting and compulsively listenable. (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Peter Humphreys January 14, 2017 Oasis fans tend to fall into two camps – those that believe their debut album “Definitely Maybe” was their best work, and those that think their monster follow up, “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory” took the cake. (Maybe there are some people who came late on the scene who put in a good word for “Dig Out Your Soul”, or “Don’t Believe the Truth”, but I haven’t met them.) I am squarely in the “Morning Glory” camp. Yes, “Definitely Maybe” was a wonderfully sharp rocker, but “Morning Glory” defined a genre. Whenever anyone talks about Britpop, you can’t do it without talking about this album – it is the benchmark. There would be no Britpop if Oasis had stopped after album number one (although Britrock maybe?). And as influential as Blur, Suede and Pulp were to the genre and to popular music generally, even though they all had albums predating Oasis, they weren’t really part of the movement until “Morning Glory” came along. “Morning Glory” gave Britpop momentum. “Morning Glory” has a particular sound, amazingly fresh when you consider how much Noel Gallagher borrowed from others – the wonderful “Don’t Look Back In Anger” leads to a towering chorus that John Lennon’s “Imagine” never got close to achieving, despite the two songs starting with the same piano riff, and Gary Glitter gets co-writing credits on opening track “Hello”, presumably so Noel Gallagher could avoid yet another songwriter taking him to court for pinching one of their songs. Each song is different, and is strong enough to be a hit (if you ignore the two 60-second untitled instrumental tracks), but each one feels like it belongs on the album, and that it is a perfect marriage of music and lyrics. When it comes to it, an album is an entity, designed to be heard in its entirety – yet an album of popular music needs to be able to be broken down into individual songs that are strong enough to stand alone. “Morning Glory” is one of those rare beasts that succeeds on both levels, and one that will always have defined a genre of its time. Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine If Definitely Maybe was an unintentional concept album about wanting to be a rock & roll star, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? is what happens after the dreams come true. Oasis turns in a relatively introspective second record, filled with big, gorgeous ballads instead of ripping rockers. Unlike Definitely Maybe, the production on Morning Glory is varied enough to handle the range in emotions; instead of drowning everything with amplifiers turned up to 12, there are strings, keyboards, and harmonicas. This expanded production helps give Noel Gallagher 's sweeping melodies an emotional resonance that he occasionally can't convey lyrically. However, that is far from a fatal flaw; Gallagher 's lyrics work best in fragments, where the images catch in your mind and grow, thanks to the music. Gallagher may be guilty of some borrowing, or even plagiarism, but he uses the familiar riffs as building blocks. This is where his genius lies: He's a thief and doesn't have many original thoughts, but as a pop/rock melodicist he's pretty much without peer. Likewise, as musicians, Oasis are hardly innovators, yet they have a majestic grandeur in their sound that makes ballads like "Wonderwall" or rockers like "Some Might Say" positively transcendent. Alan White does add authority to the rhythm section, but the most noticeable change is in Liam Gallagher . His voice sneered throughout Definitely Maybe, but on Morning Glory his singing has become more textured and skillful. He gives the lyric in the raging title track a hint of regret, is sympathetic on "Wonderwall," defiant on "Some Might Say," and humorous on "She's Electric," a bawdy rewrite of "Digsy's Diner." It might not have the immediate impact of Definitely Maybe, but Morning Glory is just as exciting and compulsively listenable. (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Peter Humphreys January 14, 2017 Oasis fans tend to fall into two camps – those that believe their debut album “Definitely Maybe” was their best work, and those that think their monster follow up, “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory” took the cake. (Maybe there are some people who came late on the scene who put in a good word for “Dig Out Your Soul”, or “Don’t Believe the Truth”, but I haven’t met them.) I am squarely in the “Morning Glory” camp. Yes, “Definitely Maybe” was a wonderfully sharp rocker, but “Morning Glory” defined a genre. Whenever anyone talks about Britpop, you can’t do it without talking about this album – it is the benchmark. There would be no Britpop if Oasis had stopped after album number one (although Britrock maybe?). And as influential as Blur, Suede and Pulp were to the genre and to popular music generally, even though they all had albums predating Oasis, they weren’t really part of the movement until “Morning Glory” came along. “Morning Glory” gave Britpop momentum. “Morning Glory” has a particular sound, amazingly fresh when you consider how much Noel Gallagher borrowed from others – the wonderful “Don’t Look Back In Anger” leads to a towering chorus that John Lennon’s “Imagine” never got close to achieving, despite the two songs starting with the same piano riff, and Gary Glitter gets co-writing credits on opening track “Hello”, presumably so Noel Gallagher could avoid yet another songwriter taking him to court for pinching one of their songs. Each song is different, and is strong enough to be a hit (if you ignore the two 60-second untitled instrumental tracks), but each one feels like it belongs on the album, and that it is a perfect marriage of music and lyrics. When it comes to it, an album is an entity, designed to be heard in its entirety – yet an album of popular music needs to be able to be broken down into individual songs that are strong enough to stand alone. “Morning Glory” is one of those rare beasts that succeeds on both levels, and one that will always have defined a genre of its time. "Cast No Shadow" has a very prominent bassline which I appreciate, but the melody seems to be repeated too many times. Alan's decision to use hot rods as he did on Wonderwall is a very nice touch. "She's Electric" sounds like a straight Beatles outtake, however Liam delivers once again. Next is "Morning Glory," which is a rocking song, but suffers from the most brickwalling in audio history. Towards the end of the song everything sounds like it is being crushed and distorted like crazy. You can also barely hear the drums, with no punch. It feels like Owen Morris, the producer, took ambience and reverb over definition, utilizing lots of room mics or mixing them much higher than close ones. Again, Liam sounds monstrous and absolutely carries the track. The album ends with "Champagne Supernova" which is a perfect ending. Paul Weller carries this track, but the lyrics prevent it from being a classic for me. The swirl at the end is perfect though and HERE there is appropriate punch on Alan's drums. That's what happens when Noel doesn't leave 20 tracks of guitar and actually gives space. Overall, the audio quality on this album is INSANELY compressed. There is no dynamic range in Liam's vocals, but that fits his in-your-face style of singing. This doesn't take away from the fact that this album is filled with great songs, but prevents it from deserving a 5 star review. Was this review helpful? Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine If Definitely Maybe was an unintentional concept album about wanting to be a rock & roll star, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? is what happens after the dreams come true. Oasis turns in a relatively introspective second record, filled with big, gorgeous ballads instead of ripping rockers. Unlike Definitely Maybe, the production on Morning Glory is varied enough to handle the range in emotions; instead of drowning everything with amplifiers turned up to 12, there are strings, keyboards, and harmonicas. This expanded production helps give Noel Gallagher 's sweeping melodies an emotional resonance that he occasionally can't convey lyrically. However, that is far from a fatal flaw; Gallagher 's lyrics work best in fragments, where the images catch in your mind and grow, thanks to the music. Gallagher may be guilty of some borrowing, or even plagiarism, but he uses the familiar riffs as building blocks. This is where his genius lies: He's a thief and doesn't have many original thoughts, but as a pop/rock melodicist he's pretty much without peer. Likewise, as musicians, Oasis are hardly innovators, yet they have a majestic grandeur in their sound that makes ballads like "Wonderwall" or rockers like "Some Might Say" positively transcendent. Alan White does add authority to the rhythm section, but the most noticeable change is in Liam Gallagher . His voice sneered throughout Definitely Maybe, but on Morning Glory his singing has become more textured and skillful. He gives the lyric in the raging title track a hint of regret, is sympathetic on "Wonderwall," defiant on "Some Might Say," and humorous on "She's Electric," a bawdy rewrite of "Digsy's Diner." It might not have the immediate impact of Definitely Maybe, but Morning Glory is just as exciting and compulsively listenable. (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Peter Humphreys January 14, 2017 Oasis fans tend to fall into two camps – those that believe their debut album “Definitely Maybe” was their best work, and those that think their monster follow up, “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory” took the cake. (Maybe there are some people who came late on the scene who put in a good word for “Dig Out Your Soul”, or “Don’t Believe the Truth”, but I haven’t met them.) I am squarely in the “Morning Glory” camp. Yes, “Definitely Maybe” was a wonderfully sharp rocker, but “Morning Glory” defined a genre. Whenever anyone talks about Britpop, you can’t do it without talking about this album – it is the benchmark. There would be no Britpop if Oasis had stopped after album number one (although Britrock maybe?). And as influential as Blur, Suede and Pulp were to the genre and to popular music generally, even though they all had albums predating Oasis, they weren’t really part of the movement until “Morning Glory” came along. “Morning Glory” gave Britpop momentum. “Morning Glory” has a particular sound, amazingly fresh when you consider how much Noel Gallagher borrowed from others – the wonderful “Don’t Look Back In Anger” leads to a towering chorus that John Lennon’s “Imagine” never got close to achieving, despite the two songs starting with the same piano riff, and Gary Glitter gets co-writing credits on opening track “Hello”, presumably so Noel Gallagher could avoid yet another songwriter taking him to court for pinching one of their songs. Each song is different, and is strong enough to be a hit (if you ignore the two 60-second untitled instrumental tracks), but each one feels like it belongs on the album, and that it is a perfect marriage of music and lyrics. When it comes to it, an album is an entity, designed to be heard in its entirety – yet an album of popular music needs to be able to be broken down into individual songs that are strong enough to stand alone. “Morning Glory” is one of those rare beasts that succeeds on both levels, and one that will always have defined a genre of its time. The melody is overwhelmingly cheesy, but Alan White's drum work is good. "Wonderwall" is obviously Oasis' most popular song, and it really does not have any flaws. I love how the bass isolated is so crunchy and distorted, but sounds great in the mix. Liam's vocals are right in your face and are sung with such attitude. "Don't Look Back in Anger" is next, which in my opinion is Oasis' best song. Everything about this song is perfect. Noel's vocal sounds aggressive yet graceful, making for a rocking ballad. After this is "Hey Now!", which is undeniably a weak point. It is too long, however the lyrics are enjoyable and easy to understand, even with Liam's Lydon-esque snarl and Mancunian accent. Next is "Some Might Say." This song is great aside from Tony McCarroll's drumming. Liam sounds insane, probably one of the biggest highlights of his vocal career. "Cast No Shadow" has a very prominent bassline which I appreciate, but the melody seems to be repeated too many times. Alan's decision to use hot rods as he did on Wonderwall is a very nice touch. "She's Electric" sounds like a straight Beatles outtake, however Liam delivers once again. Next is "Morning Glory," which is a rocking song, but suffers from the most brickwalling in audio history. Towards the end of the song everything sounds like it is being crushed and distorted like crazy. You can also barely hear the drums, with no punch. There is no dynamic range in Liam's vocals, but that fits his in-your-face style of singing. Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine If Definitely Maybe was an unintentional concept album about wanting to be a rock & roll star, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? is what happens after the dreams come true. Oasis turns in a relatively introspective second record, filled with big, gorgeous ballads instead of ripping rockers. Unlike Definitely Maybe, the production on Morning Glory is varied enough to handle the range in emotions; instead of drowning everything with amplifiers turned up to 12, there are strings, keyboards, and harmonicas. This expanded production helps give Noel Gallagher 's sweeping melodies an emotional resonance that he occasionally can't convey lyrically. However, that is far from a fatal flaw; Gallagher 's lyrics work best in fragments, where the images catch in your mind and grow, thanks to the music. Gallagher may be guilty of some borrowing, or even plagiarism, but he uses the familiar riffs as building blocks. This is where his genius lies: He's a thief and doesn't have many original thoughts, but as a pop/rock melodicist he's pretty much without peer. Likewise, as musicians, Oasis are hardly innovators, yet they have a majestic grandeur in their sound that makes ballads like "Wonderwall" or rockers like "Some Might Say" positively transcendent. Alan White does add authority to the rhythm section, but the most noticeable change is in Liam Gallagher . His voice sneered throughout Definitely Maybe, but on Morning Glory his singing has become more textured and skillful. He gives the lyric in the raging title track a hint of regret, is sympathetic on "Wonderwall," defiant on "Some Might Say," and humorous on "She's Electric," a bawdy rewrite of "Digsy's Diner." It might not have the immediate impact of Definitely Maybe, but Morning Glory is just as exciting and compulsively listenable. (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Peter Humphreys January 14, 2017 Oasis fans tend to fall into two camps – those that believe their debut album “Definitely Maybe” was their best work, and those that think their monster follow up, “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory” took the cake. (Maybe there are some people who came late on the scene who put in a good word for “Dig Out Your Soul”, or “Don’t Believe the Truth”, but I haven’t met them.) I am squarely in the “Morning Glory” camp. Yes, “Definitely Maybe” was a wonderfully sharp rocker, but “Morning Glory” defined a genre. Whenever anyone talks about Britpop, you can’t do it without talking about this album – it is the benchmark. There would be no Britpop if Oasis had stopped after album number one (although Britrock maybe?). And as influential as Blur, Suede and Pulp were to the genre and to popular music generally, even though they all had albums predating Oasis, they weren’t really part of the movement until “Morning Glory” came along. “Morning Glory” gave Britpop momentum. “Morning Glory” has a particular sound, amazingly fresh when you consider how much Noel Gallagher borrowed from others – the wonderful “Don’t Look Back In Anger” leads to a towering chorus that John Lennon’s “Imagine” never got close to achieving, despite the two songs starting with the same piano riff, and Gary Glitter gets co-writing credits on opening track “Hello”, presumably so Noel Gallagher could avoid yet another songwriter taking him to court for pinching one of their songs. Each song is different, and is strong enough to be a hit (if you ignore the two 60-second untitled instrumental tracks), but each one feels like it belongs on the album, and that it is a perfect marriage of music and lyrics. When it comes to it, an album is an entity, designed to be heard in its entirety – yet an album of popular music needs to be able to be broken down into individual songs that are strong enough to stand alone. “Morning Glory” is one of those rare beasts that succeeds on both levels, and one that will always have defined a genre of its time. Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine If Definitely Maybe was an unintentional concept album about wanting to be a rock & roll star, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? is what happens after the dreams come true. Oasis turns in a relatively introspective second record, filled with big, gorgeous ballads instead of ripping rockers. Unlike Definitely Maybe, the production on Morning Glory is varied enough to handle the range in emotions; instead of drowning everything with amplifiers turned up to 12, there are strings, keyboards, and harmonicas. This expanded production helps give Noel Gallagher 's sweeping melodies an emotional resonance that he occasionally can't convey lyrically. However, that is far from a fatal flaw; Gallagher 's lyrics work best in fragments, where the images catch in your mind and grow, thanks to the music. Gallagher may be guilty of some borrowing, or even plagiarism, but he uses the familiar riffs as building blocks. This is where his genius lies: He's a thief and doesn't have many original thoughts, but as a pop/rock melodicist he's pretty much without peer. Likewise, as musicians, Oasis are hardly innovators, yet they have a majestic grandeur in their sound that makes ballads like "Wonderwall" or rockers like "Some Might Say" positively transcendent. Alan White does add authority to the rhythm section, but the most noticeable change is in Liam Gallagher . His voice sneered throughout Definitely Maybe, but on Morning Glory his singing has become more textured and skillful. He gives the lyric in the raging title track a hint of regret, is sympathetic on "Wonderwall," defiant on "Some Might Say," and humorous on "She's Electric," a bawdy rewrite of "Digsy's Diner." It might not have the immediate impact of Definitely Maybe, but Morning Glory is just as exciting and compulsively listenable. (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Peter Humphreys January 14, 2017 Oasis fans tend to fall into two camps – those that believe their debut album “Definitely Maybe” was their best work, and those that think their monster follow up, “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory” took the cake. (Maybe there are some people who came late on the scene who put in a good word for “Dig Out Your Soul”, or “Don’t Believe the Truth”, but I haven’t met them.) I am squarely in the “Morning Glory” camp. Yes, “Definitely Maybe” was a wonderfully sharp rocker, but “Morning Glory” defined a genre. Whenever anyone talks about Britpop, you can’t do it without talking about this album – it is the benchmark. There would be no Britpop if Oasis had stopped after album number one (although Britrock maybe?). And as influential as Blur, Suede and Pulp were to the genre and to popular music generally, even though they all had albums predating Oasis, they weren’t really part of the movement until “Morning Glory” came along. “Morning Glory” gave Britpop momentum. “Morning Glory” has a particular sound, amazingly fresh when you consider how much Noel Gallagher borrowed from others – the wonderful “Don’t Look Back In Anger” leads to a towering chorus that John Lennon’s “Imagine” never got close to achieving, despite the two songs starting with the same piano riff, and Gary Glitter gets co-writing credits on opening track “Hello”, presumably so Noel Gallagher could avoid yet another songwriter taking him to court for pinching one of their songs. Each song is different, and is strong enough to be a hit (if you ignore the two 60-second untitled instrumental tracks), but each one feels like it belongs on the album, and that it is a perfect marriage of music and lyrics. When it comes to it, an album is an entity, designed to be heard in its entirety – yet an album of popular music needs to be able to be broken down into individual songs that are strong enough to stand alone. “Morning Glory” is one of those rare beasts that succeeds on both levels, and one that will always have defined a genre of its time. Paul Weller carries this track, but the lyrics prevent it from being a classic for me. The swirl at the end is perfect though and HERE there is appropriate punch on Alan's drums. Review by Stephen Thomas Erlewine If Definitely Maybe was an unintentional concept album about wanting to be a rock & roll star, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? is what happens after the dreams come true. Oasis turns in a relatively introspective second record, filled with big, gorgeous ballads instead of ripping rockers. Unlike Definitely Maybe, the production on Morning Glory is varied enough to handle the range in emotions; instead of drowning everything with amplifiers turned up to 12, there are strings, keyboards, and harmonicas. This expanded production helps give Noel Gallagher 's sweeping melodies an emotional resonance that he occasionally can't convey lyrically. However, that is far from a fatal flaw; Gallagher 's lyrics work best in fragments, where the images catch in your mind and grow, thanks to the music. Gallagher may be guilty of some borrowing, or even plagiarism, but he uses the familiar riffs as building blocks. This is where his genius lies: He's a thief and doesn't have many original thoughts, but as a pop/rock melodicist he's pretty much without peer. Likewise, as musicians, Oasis are hardly innovators, yet they have a majestic grandeur in their sound that makes ballads like "Wonderwall" or rockers like "Some Might Say" positively transcendent. Alan White does add authority to the rhythm section, but the most noticeable change is in Liam Gallagher . His voice sneered throughout Definitely Maybe, but on Morning Glory his singing has become more textured and skillful. He gives the lyric in the raging title track a hint of regret, is sympathetic on "Wonderwall," defiant on "Some Might Say," and humorous on "She's Electric," a bawdy rewrite of "Digsy's Diner." It might not have the immediate impact of Definitely Maybe, but Morning Glory is just as exciting and compulsively listenable. (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Peter Humphreys January 14, 2017 Oasis fans tend to fall into two camps – those that believe their debut album “Definitely Maybe” was their best work, and those that think their monster follow up, “(What’s the Story) Morning Glory” took the cake. (Maybe there are some people who came late on the scene who put in a good word for “Dig Out Your Soul”, or “Don’t Believe the Truth”, but I haven’t met them.) I am squarely in the “Morning Glory” camp. Yes, “Definitely Maybe” was a wonderfully sharp rocker, but “Morning Glory” defined a genre. Whenever anyone talks about Britpop, you can’t do it without talking about this album – it is the benchmark. There would be no Britpop if Oasis had stopped after album number one (although Britrock maybe?). And as influential as Blur, Suede and Pulp were to the genre and to popular music generally, even though they all had albums predating Oasis, they weren’t really part of the movement until “Morning Glory” came along. “Morning Glory” gave Britpop momentum. “Morning Glory” has a particular sound, amazingly fresh when you consider how much Noel Gallagher borrowed from others – the wonderful “Don’t Look Back In Anger” leads to a towering chorus that John Lennon’s “Imagine” never got close to achieving, despite the two songs starting with the same piano riff, and Gary Glitter gets co-writing credits on opening track “Hello”, presumably so Noel Gallagher could avoid yet another songwriter taking him to court for pinching one of their songs. Each song is different, and is strong enough to be a hit (if you ignore the two 60-second untitled instrumental tracks), but each one feels like it belongs on the album, and that it is a perfect marriage of music and lyrics. When it comes to it, an album is an entity, designed to be heard in its entirety – yet an album of popular music needs to be able to be broken down into individual songs that are strong enough to stand alone. “Morning Glory” is one of those rare beasts that succeeds on both levels, and one that will always have defined a genre of its time.
